title: Cross-language traps
description: Production bugs whose shape depends on the language: a rounding helper that is not symmetric for negative money, doubles whose == and equals disagree on NaN and negative zero, and text truncated to a UTF-8 byte budget without splitting a character. Each drill ends with a "Same bug elsewhere" paragraph on how C# and JavaScript differ; the byte-budget drill has a C# twin with the same vectors (csdrills 06/09). Only traps that are new to the Java estate are here: idempotency keys, pagination bounds, DST arithmetic, int-overflow totals and shared mutable defaults are already taught by javabootcamp (10/08, 19/02, 19/08, 01/06, 19/04).

exercises.title: Half-even vs half-up on negative money
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our ledger stores amounts in mills (tenths of a cent). The invoice helper converts to cents — and the refund of a charge no longer matches the charge. Find the bug and make both rounding modes work."

**Why it works.** The shipped helper uses `Math.round(mills / 10.0)`. `Math.round(x)` is `floor(x + 0.5)`: it rounds every half toward **+∞**, so `1234.5` becomes `1235` but `-1234.5` becomes `-1234`. Charges and refunds stop mirroring each other, it ignores the requested mode, and it is never half-even. Going through `double` also hides the fact that the input is an EXACT decimal. `BigDecimal` can hold `mills / 10` exactly and round it with a NAMED `RoundingMode`: there, `HALF_UP` means half **away from zero** (symmetric for refunds), `HALF_EVEN` (banker's rounding) sends exact halves to the even neighbour, and `UP` — a different mode — would round EVERY fraction away from zero.

**Your task.** Fix `toCents(long mills, Mode mode)`:
- `HALF_EVEN`: exact halves go to the even neighbour; anything else to the nearest cent.
- `HALF_UP`: exact halves go away from zero; anything else to the nearest cent.
- Positive and negative amounts must round symmetrically in both modes.

**Worked example.** `toCents(12345, HALF_EVEN)` is `1234`, `toCents(12345, HALF_UP)` is `1235`, `toCents(-12345, HALF_UP)` is `-1235`.

**Same bug elsewhere.** In C# the helper fails on different rows: `Math.Round` defaults to `MidpointRounding.ToEven`, so `Math.Round(mills / 10.0)` passes half-even and breaks half-up — csdrills 04/02 (midpoint-rounding) is the C# drill on that default. Java's `Math.round` instead breaks half-up on negative halves (`-12345` gives `-1234`) and half-even on positive ones (`12345` gives `1235`). In JavaScript, `Math.round(-1234.5)` is also `-1234`: it rounds halves toward +∞ exactly like Java's.
exercises.explanation:
Name the rounding rule; never inherit one from a float helper.

- `12345` mills = 1234.5 cents: half-even → 1234 (4 is even), half-up → 1235. The shipped `Math.round` gives 1235 for both modes, so the half-even row fails.
- `-12345` = -1234.5: half-even → -1234, half-up → -1235 (away from zero). `Math.round` gives -1234 for both: right for half-even by luck, wrong for half-up.
- `-12355` = -1235.5: half-even → -1236 (6 is even); `Math.round` gives -1235.
- `12344` = 1234.4 → 1234 and `-12346` = -1234.6 → -1235 in half-up: only exact halves move away from zero. `RoundingMode.UP` would give 1235 for `12344` — that is a different rule.

The fix: `BigDecimal.valueOf(mills, 1)` is exactly `mills / 10`; `setScale(0, mode)` with `RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN` or `RoundingMode.HALF_UP` rounds it; `longValueExact()` reads it back.

Kinship: javadrills 08/02 (line vs invoice rounding) and 08/06 (banker's rounding on cross rates) choose WHERE to round; this drill is about the sign-symmetry trap in the rounding helper itself, the bug that makes refunds disagree with charges.
hints: Run the failing tests and compare a charge with its refund: Math.round is not symmetric for negative halves, ignores the mode and is never half-even.
BigDecimal can represent the mills divided by ten exactly, and its setScale takes a RoundingMode; check which RoundingMode constant means half away from zero.
build the exact decimal of the mills at scale one, rescale it to whole cents with the rounding mode the caller asked for, and read it back as an exact long

exercises.title: The reading that never equals itself
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "Our sensor feed marks missing readings as NaN and the 'missing' counter is stuck at zero. The dashboard also shows `0.0` and `-0.0` as two different readings. Explain both, then fix the helpers."

**Why it works.** `double` follows IEEE 754, and Java's two notions of equality disagree on exactly two values:
- `==` says `NaN == NaN` is **false** (NaN is unequal to everything, itself included), so `x == Double.NaN` is never true. `Double.isNaN(x)` is the test.
- `==` says `0.0 == -0.0` is **true**, but `Double.equals` and `Double.compare` tell them apart — and `Double.equals` says NaN equals NaN.

Collections use `equals`/`hashCode` (and sorted ones `compareTo`), so a `HashSet<Double>` keeps `0.0` and `-0.0` as two elements but all NaNs as one. A tiny negative value rounded to zero becomes `-0.0` and prints as `-0.0`. `Double.compare` is also the total order `List.sort` needs: `-0.0` before `0.0`, NaN after everything. A comparator built from `<` and `>` treats NaN as "equal" to every number and breaks the sort contract.

**Your task.** Implement:
- `isMissing(double reading)` → true exactly for NaN.
- `canonical(double reading)` → the grouping key: `-0.0` becomes `0.0`; every other value, NaN included, is unchanged.
- `distinctReadings(List<Double> readings)` → the number of distinct readings when `0.0` and `-0.0` are the same reading and every NaN is the same missing value.
- `ascending(List<Double> readings)` → a sorted copy: `-0.0` before `0.0`, NaN last.

**Worked example.** `distinctReadings(List.of(0.0, -0.0, 1.5, 1.5))` is **2**, and `isMissing(0.0 / 0.0)` is true.

**Same bug elsewhere.** JavaScript has the same IEEE values but different collection rules: `NaN === NaN` is false and `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true, `Object.is(0, -0)` is false, and `Set`/`Map` use SameValueZero, which treats all NaNs as one key AND `0` and `-0` as one key — the dedupe that needs a canonical key in Java comes for free there. In C#, `double.NaN == double.NaN` is false but `double.NaN.Equals(double.NaN)` is true, as in Java — yet C#'s `Equals` and `HashSet<double>` treat `0.0` and `-0.0` as the same value, so there, as in JavaScript, the canonical zero key is a chore only Java needs.
exercises.explanation:
Two equalities, two different answers.

For `distinctReadings(List.of(0.0, -0.0, 1.5, 1.5))`:
- boxed into a `HashSet<Double>` as they are: `Double.equals(0.0, -0.0)` is false (their bit patterns differ), so the set holds `0.0`, `-0.0`, `1.5` → 3
- after `canonical`, `-0.0` has become `0.0` (`-0.0 == 0.0` is true, so `reading == 0.0 ? 0.0 : reading` folds both) → the set holds `0.0`, `1.5` → **2**
- NaNs need no folding for the set: `Double.equals` compares `doubleToLongBits`, which maps every NaN to one canonical pattern, so `NaN` and `0.0 / 0.0` count once

For `isMissing`, `reading == Double.NaN` is false for every input, NaN included; `Double.isNaN` is the only reliable test. For `ascending`, `Double::compare` gives the total order `[-1.0, -0.0, 0.0, 1.0, NaN]`, while `(a, b) -> a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0` says NaN equals every number and leaves NaN wherever it started.

Kinship: javabootcamp 01's README notes that `0.0 / 0` is NaN and that NaN equals nothing, and its sealed-types module rejects NaN as input; this drill is the equality and ordering consequences when NaN and `-0.0` are values you must keep. In an interview, "`==` for doubles is IEEE, `equals`/`compare` is for collections" is the sentence.
hints: Print 0.0 / 0.0 == 0.0 / 0.0 and Double.valueOf(0.0).equals(-0.0) before writing anything.
Double.isNaN tests for NaN; -0.0 == 0.0 is true, so a comparison with zero can fold negative zero; Double.compare is a total order that a sort can use.
test for the missing marker with the dedicated NaN check, fold negative zero by comparing against zero, deduplicate the folded values in a hash set, and sort a copy with the total order on doubles

exercises.title: Truncate to a byte budget
exercises.instructions:
**Interview prompt.** "The `display_name` column holds at most 32 BYTES of UTF-8. We truncated with `substring(0, 32)` and the database still rejected names — and one name came back with a `?` at the end. Truncate correctly."

**Why it works.** A Java `String` counts UTF-16 units, and `length()` says nothing about the encoded size. In UTF-8 a code point takes 1 byte (U+0000-U+007F), 2 bytes (up to U+07FF, e.g. `é`), 3 bytes (up to U+FFFF, e.g. `€`) or 4 bytes (above, e.g. `🙂`, which is ALSO two `char`s in Java). So `"café"` is 4 chars but 5 bytes. Cutting the encoded bytes at the limit can split a multi-byte character, and decoding the cut bytes produces a replacement character. Cutting by `char` can split a surrogate pair. The safe method walks whole code points (`codePointAt`, `Character.charCount`), adds each one's UTF-8 size, and stops before the first one that would not fit.

**Your task.** Implement:
- `utf8Length(String s)` → the number of bytes in `s`'s UTF-8 encoding.
- `truncateUtf8(String s, int maxBytes)` → the longest prefix of `s` whose UTF-8 encoding has at most `maxBytes` bytes and that never splits a code point; a negative `maxBytes` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Inputs are well-formed (no unpaired surrogates).

**Worked example.** `truncateUtf8("café", 4)` is `"caf"` (the `é` needs 2 more bytes), and `truncateUtf8("a🙂b", 5)` is `"a🙂"` (1 + 4 bytes).

**Same bug elsewhere.** csdrills 06/09 (utf8-byte-budget) is the same contract with the same vectors in C#, where `Length` also counts UTF-16 units and `Encoding.UTF8.GetByteCount` counts bytes. The two runtimes disagree on malformed input: Java's `getBytes(UTF_8)` encodes an unpaired surrogate as one `?` byte (`3F`), while .NET writes the three-byte replacement character (`EF BF BD`) — so a byte count computed per `char` is wrong in a different way in each language. In JavaScript, `s.length` counts UTF-16 units too, and `new TextEncoder().encode(s).length` counts the bytes.
exercises.explanation:
Budget in bytes, step in code points.

For `truncateUtf8("a🙂b", 5)`:
- `a` is U+0061 → 1 byte, total 1 ≤ 5 → keep it, move 1 char
- `🙂` is U+1F642 → 4 bytes, total 5 ≤ 5 → keep it, move 2 chars (the surrogate pair)
- `b` → total 6 > 5 → stop: the prefix is `"a🙂"` (3 chars, 5 bytes)

With a budget of 4 the emoji would make 5 bytes, so only `"a"` survives — the pair is kept or dropped whole. The shortcuts fail on these rows: `substring(0, maxBytes)` keeps `"café"` (5 bytes) for a budget of 4; cutting the encoded bytes and decoding gives `"caf"` followed by U+FFFD; counting each `char` separately counts a lone surrogate as one byte (`?`), so a budget of 2 keeps `"a"` plus half an emoji.

Kinship: the code-points drill of the strings module counts code points versus `char`s; this drill adds the third measure, encoded bytes, and the truncation that respects all three. In an interview, "which length — chars, code points or bytes?" is the question to ask first.
hints: Three different lengths are in play: UTF-16 chars, code points and UTF-8 bytes, and the column limit is the last one.
String.getBytes with StandardCharsets.UTF_8 gives the encoded bytes; String.codePointAt and Character.charCount step one whole character at a time.
walk the string one code point at a time, add the one to four bytes each needs, stop before the first that would overflow the budget, and cut the string at that position
